verses.text: He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood. It was square. Its length was five cubits,  its width was five cubits, and its height was three cubits.
He made its horns on its four corners. Its horns were of one piece with it, and he overlaid it with brass.
He made all the vessels of the altar, the pots, the shovels, the basins, the forks, and the fire pans. He made all its vessels of brass.
He made for the altar a grating of a network of brass, under the ledge around it beneath, reaching halfway up.
He cast four rings for the four ends of brass grating, to be places for the poles.
He made the poles of acacia wood, and overlaid them with brass.
He put the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar, with which to carry it. He made it hollow with planks.
He made the basin of brass, and its base of brass, out of the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
He made the court: for the south side southward the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, one hundred cubits;
their pillars were twenty, and their sockets twenty, of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver.
For the north side one hundred cubits, their pillars twenty, and their sockets twenty, of brass; the hooks of the pillars, and their fillets, of silver.
For the west side were hangings of fifty cubits, their pillars ten, and their sockets ten; the hooks of the pillars, and their fillets, of silver.
For the east side eastward fifty cubits.
The hangings for the one side were fifteen cubits; their pillars three, and their sockets three;
and so for the other side: on this hand and that hand by the gate of the court were hangings of fifteen cubits; their pillars three, and their sockets three.
All the hangings around the court were of fine twined linen.

The sockets for the pillars were of brass. The hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver; and the overlaying of their capitals, of silver; and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver.

The screen for the gate of the court was the work of the embroiderer, of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. Twenty cubits was the length, and the height in the width was five cubits, like to the hangings of the court.
Their pillars were four, and their sockets four, of brass; their hooks of silver, and the overlaying of their capitals, and their fillets, of silver.
All the pins of the tabernacle, and around the court, were of brass.

This is the amount of material used for the tabernacle, even the Tabernacle of the Testimony, as they were counted, according to the commandment of Moses, for the service of the Levites, by the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest.
Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that Yahweh commanded Moses.
With him was Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver, and a skillful workman, and an embroiderer in blue, in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen.

All the gold that was used for the work in all the work of the sanctuary, even the gold of the offering, was twenty-nine talents,  and seven hundred thirty shekels, after the shekel  of the sanctuary.
The silver of those who were counted of the congregation was one hundred talents,  and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels,  after the shekel of the sanctuary:

a beka  a head, that is, half a shekel, after the shekel  of the sanctuary, for everyone who passed over to those who were counted, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty men.
The one hundred talents  of silver were for casting the sockets of the sanctuary, and the sockets of the veil; one hundred sockets for the one hundred talents, a talent for a socket.
Of the one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels  he made hooks for the pillars, overlaid their capitals, and made fillets for them.
The brass of the offering was seventy talents,  and two thousand four hundred shekels.
With this he made the sockets to the door of the Tent of Meeting, the bronze altar, the bronze grating for it, all the vessels of the altar,
the sockets around the court, the sockets of the gate of the court, all the pins of the tabernacle, and all the pins around the court.

footnotes.content: The altar is built to precise dimensions—five cubits by five, three high—a square foundation. Notice how exactness matters even in the place where blood flows and fire burns. Jesus, in His sacrifice, fulfilled what this altar could only point toward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four horns rise from the corners—carved from the wood itself, not separately attached. These horns become places of refuge in the law; they speak to how God's provision is woven into the very structure of His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every tool has its purpose: pots for ash, shovels for removal, basins for water, forks for the wood, fire pans for coals. God's house teaches us that faithful work, even the unglamorous parts, is sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The grating sits halfway up the altar—a network of brass that holds the fire, that allows ash to fall through and air to reach below. What looks like a simple grid serves a profound purpose: separation and purification.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four rings, one for each corner—places where the poles would rest. Even these small fasteners are counted and placed with intention. God's attention to detail reminds us that He notices what we think is hidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Acacia wood overlaid with brass—sturdy and lasting, shielded from decay. The poles that carry the altar's weight are themselves strengthened, teaching us that what bears heavy burdens must be fortified by God's provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The altar is hollow inside—made of planks, not solid mass. What matters is the opening: the place where fire meets sacrifice, where heaven and earth draw near. The emptiness itself holds the holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The basin is forged from the mirrors of the women who served at the Tent's door—their bronze polished smooth turned into a vessel for washing. God treasures the devotion of those who serve quietly, and transforms even their personal gifts into instruments of holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The south side: one hundred cubits of fine linen hanging, a barrier and a boundary. The court encloses the sacred, not to hide it but to mark the place where God dwells with His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty pillars set in brass sockets, with silver hooks and fillets—a framework of strength and beauty. Even the support system itself speaks of God's glory: nothing is left merely functional when the aim is to house His presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: North side, same length as the south—a symmetry that speaks to balance and order. God's sanctuary reflects the ordered beauty of His creation; all is aligned by His design.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The west side, fifty cubits—shorter than the long sides. The court takes its shape, each side fitted to its purpose. There is no waste in God's design, only wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty cubits eastward—the same breadth as the west. The east faces the rising sun, the place where light first breaks. Even the direction speaks: God's dwelling opens toward the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifteen cubits on one side of the gate; three pillars holding the opening. The entrance itself requires framing, strength, and proportion—nothing careless in the way we approach God's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifteen cubits on this hand and that hand by the gate—the opening is framed on both sides with equal care. The gate of the court becomes a threshold of symmetry: enter here, to a place of sacred balance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the hangings around the court, fine twined linen—a single material unites the whole enclosure. What a picture of unity: one cloth, one court, one people gathered around their God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Brass sockets hold the pillars; silver hooks and fillets crown them—precious metals woven through the structure. God values both what is hidden (the sockets bearing weight) and what is seen (the silver polish at eye level). All work honors Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gate screen is embroidered: blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen—colors that recall the priestly garments and the veil of the inner sanctuary. The place where people enter to meet God is adorned with the same splendor that marks His presence within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four pillars frame the gate, their capitals overlaid with silver—a doorway both humble and grand. To enter the court of the Lord requires passage through a threshold that declares both the sanctity of what lies beyond and the welcome of the open gate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the pins—every stake that holds the tent fast to the earth—are brass. Small things, easily overlooked, yet necessary. God does not despise the small acts of faithfulness that keep His people secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This accounting is made 'according to the commandment of Moses, for the service of the Levites, by the hand of Ithamar'—meticulous, official, ordered. The work of building God's house is done with care, oversight, and a clear chain of responsibility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bezalel of Judah made all that the Lord commanded—a man equipped with skill, given a task, and faithful to complete it. His name means 'in the shadow of God'; he worked in the shelter of God's calling and accomplished all that was laid before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Oholiab of Dan joined him—skilled in engraving, weaving, embroidery. Two craftsmen from different tribes, united in one work. The sanctuary is built not by one gifted hand but by the cooperation of diverse talents all bent toward God's purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-nine talents of gold plus seven hundred thirty shekels—a precise and stunning sum. The weight speaks: God's house receives the precious, the weighty, the best that His people can bring. Yet even this immense treasure is merely the foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred talents of silver from the congregation—vast wealth gathered through a redemption tax. Every soul counted, every soul contributing. This silver becomes the true bones of the sanctuary: the sockets on which everything rests.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Half a shekel per person—a beka—collected from six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty men. Each contribution is equal, each soul matters equally in the building of God's house. No one gives less because they are poor; no one is exempted because they are small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred talents of silver cast into sockets for the sanctuary and the veil—exactly matched, one talent per socket. The mathematics of holiness: everything accounted for, nothing wasted, all aligned with precision and purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The remaining seventeen hundred seventy-five shekels became hooks for the pillars, capitals overlaid, and fillets—the finishing work. Even the leftovers are transformed into beauty. God wastes nothing; all is refined into its appointed place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy talents of brass plus two thousand four hundred shekels—the bronze offering, strong and lasting. This metal, less precious than gold or silver, will bear the greatest weight and withstand the heat: faithful, enduring material for a faithful God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From this brass came the sockets at the Tent's door, the bronze altar, the grating, and all the vessels—the functional heart of the sanctuary. What is made to work and last is made of this sturdy metal. God provides what endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sockets around the court, the gate sockets, all the pins—the tabernacle held firm. Looking back from our time, we see how God still holds His sanctuary steady: the church, His dwelling place, rests on foundations He alone has laid. We are built into His house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
